lawyer:
Salahuddin Ahmed, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners. 
Abdur Rashid, Advocates ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Virginia Tobacco Co. Ltd. and others ----- Petitioners.
Vs.
Chairman Labor Court and others ----- Respondents.
full_judgment: 9. In the case, the respondent Nos. 2-51 sought for declaration that lay-off notice was illegal, and they were to wages and salaries. According to section 2(1), lay-off means the failure, refusal or inability off an employer on account of shortage of coal, power or raw material or die accumulation of stock or the break-down of machinery or for any other reason, to give employment worker whose name is borne on the muster-rolls to his shop, commercial establishment or industrial establishment. Section 6(1) empowers an employer at any time, in the event of fire, catastrophe, break-down of machinery, or stoppage of power supply, epidemics, civil commotion or other cause beyond his sections of the shop or the commercial or industrial  establishment, wholly or partly, for any period. Section 2(1), seems to us, empowers an employer to issue a lay-off notice, if he is satisfied that there exists any of the causes enumerated therein or for other reason. Mr. Rashid submits that in this case the lay-off notice was given on the ground of financial inability of the petitioner company which, according to him, is not a condition for which a lay-off notice can he given under section 2(1) of the Act. He submits that the expression "other reason" shall be read as ejusdem generis and "other reason" shall be of the like nature of the preceding expressions used in section 2(1) of the Act and it does not include "financial inability." So interpreting, he submits that the Respondent 1 in directing to call off lay-off notice and to pay lay-off benefits and wages to the Respondents 2-51 acted within his competency. On section 6 he submits that it also does not authorize the employer to stop an industry on the ground of "financial inability" as no such expression occurs in section 6 of the Act. On the facts of the present case, the contention does not seem to us as sound. In this case we find that the petitioner company made utmost effort in order to get necessary fund to run the industry. It made approach to different financial houses including the Government to provide financial assistance to run the industry which is evidently manifest from Annexure-D to this petition. Although the statement of the financial crisis made by the petitioners have been denied by the respondents by way of affidavit. But in view of the financial position as emerges from the balance sheet as stated above we arc of the view that the company suffered loss and was under continuing disability to make wages of the employees and staffs. Now we are to examine the soundness of the interpretation of the expression "other cause beyond his control" as given by Mr. Rashid. Whether the expression only means the event of the nature as enumerated in section 6 of the Act. We are afraid to give such a restricted interpretation to the expression as urged by Mr. Rashid inasmuch as giving such interpretation will be compelling an employer to continue to run an industry at his own peril calling for a total-liquidation of the company itself. On facts of the instant case, financial inability, in our opinion, is covered by the expression "Other cause beyond his control," used in section 6 of the Act In this context it is pertinent to observe, keeping in view the scheme of the law, which is enacted to create a good relation between the employees and the employer and to secure their respective rights, that the right of the employer to take an action under section 6 of the Act as has been taken in this case cannot feuered with such limitation. This right of the company to stop or discontinue the industry at any time, if it is. satisfied that there is no prospect to, continue the industry is available to the company and the workers for that Matter have no say in this regard and are not entitled to seek a direction from the Labour Court to open the industry by instituting a case under section 34 of the Ordinance and the Labour Court has no such power to make such order and the workers are left with no remedy except that as provided in section 9 of the Act during the period they were laid-off. Thus, we hold that the lay-off notice, in the facts and circumstances of the present case, cannot be declared to be illegal. It is interesting to note that the Labour Court having had declared the lay-off notice illegal directed the petitioner to pay the lay-off benefit etc. This shows that it failed to apply its judicial mind in passing the order impugned on due consideration of the facts and the provision of law in this respect. In this case we are satisfied from the facts that the petitioner-company was put under severe pressure by the worker to exact their illegal demands under duress. Ticking this aspect into consideration as well we hold that this event also falls within the expression cause-beyond his control and the signing of the demand; under such circumstances cannot be pleaded that the petitioner I had sound financial ability to pay wages, etc.
